approved: Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that would re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission and replace the Fair Work (Building Industry) Act 2012 with a new regime.
It would repeal the Fair Work (Building Industry) Act 2012, make minor consequential amendments to Commonwealth laws, and set out transitional rules for institutions, staff, and legal proceedings.
The bill says section 7 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901, which preserves investigations and liabilities, would not be limited by this bill.
Repeal the Fair Work (Building Industry) Act 2012.
Make minor consequential amendments to Commonwealth legislation relevant to the Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013.
Provide transitional provisions for changes of names of institutions and offices, preserving appointments of senior position holders, and preserving employment entitlements of staff.
The Australian Building and Construction Commission, staff of affected organisations, and bodies operating under the building and construction industry regime.

Introduced a companion machinery bill to manage the transition from the Fair Work Building Industry Act 2012 to the newly re-established Australian Building and Construction Commission, and to deal with residual matters under the earlier Building and Construction Industry Improvement Act 2005.

The Selection of Bills Committee recommended referring several bills to Senate committees for inquiry, including carbon tax repeal bills to report by 2 December 2013, while a proposed amendment to extend the reporting date to March 2014 was rejected.

Opposed the government's bill re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission, arguing its coercive interview and imprisonment powers compromise civil liberties, and noted Fair Work Building and Construction had already recovered more than $2 million in unpaid wages for over 1,500 workers without such powers.

Supported re-establishing the ABCC, citing his own earlier estimates that it delivered a 10 per cent productivity increase, a $5.5 billion annual welfare gain, and cut construction industry working days lost from 224 per 1,000 employees in 2004 to just 24 in 2006.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said the existing Fair Work Building and Construction regulator has already recovered over $2 million in unpaid entitlements for more than 1,500 workers, noted industrial disputation in construction is on average less than one-fifth the rate under the previous coalition government, and cited legal academics comparing the ABCC's coercive powers to those used in national security and terrorism law.

Opposed the ABCC bill, drawing on 25 years representing union members, described a workplace death his son witnessed on a WA construction site, noted the bill imposes penalties of $34,000 for individuals and $170,000 for organisations, and recalled the $70 million Cole royal commission producing not a single criminal charge.

Opposed the ABCC bill, noting the Cole royal commission that preceded the ABCC's creation in 2005 cost $66 million over 18 months but produced no criminal convictions, and criticised the bill's reverse onus provisions and $34,000 maximum penalty for unlawful picketing as excessive and a breach of international labour conventions.

Said the Building and Construction Industry bills would re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission with investigative powers restricting workers' rights of entry, representation and the right to remain silent, describing the legislation as pernicious.
